title: The 8 key storylines to follow at the Vuelta a España
content:
Cyclist
The 8 key storylines to follow at the Vuelta a España

Grand Tour season is almost over. The Vuelta a España begins in Monaco on Saturday 22nd September, heading through southern France and Andorra before reaching Spain, where it will largely be contained to the southern region of the country. Here we look at the key storylines to follow throughout the three weeks.

Tadej Pogačar chasing the triple

The last time Tadej Pogačar participated in the Vuelta came back in 2019. He grabbed his first Grand Tour stage win with victory towards Cortals d’Encamp, then claimed two more stages and finished third overall. Fast forward to 2026 and Pogačar arrives off a record-tying Tour de France victory looking for his first Vuelta win. It would put him in the special club that Jonas Vingegaard also joined this year of winning all three Grand Tours. Let’s be honest, he has one foot in the door already.

How will Primož Roglič approach the race?

In another timeline, Primož Roglič is eyeing a Vuelta victory that puts him above Roberto Heras on the all-time winners list, standing alone with five to his name. Even aside from Pogačar’s participation thwarting these plans, this has been a difficult season for the 36-year-old who hasn’t managed to make a dent on any GC in the stage races he’s entered – 5th at Tirreno-Adriatico, 16th at Itzulia Basque Country, 18th at the Tour de Romandie and 8th at the Tour de Suisse. Now granted, the majority of these results are down to either teammates Giulio Pellizzari or Florian Lipowitz finishing above him.

Even in training he can’t seen to escape misfortune. Roglič was forced to miss Clásica San Sebastián and the Vuelta a Burgos after being hit by a car. This will also be his final Grand Tour for Red Bull-Bora-Hansgrohe.

Felix Gall could match his Giro d’Italia best

Felix Gall will likely finish on the podium of the Vuelta – but where, Chris Kamara? The Austrian impressed by finishing second overall to Vingegaard at the Giro and consistently best of the rest in the mountains stages, pointing towards him being very likely to improve on his highest finish of eighth place overall in Spain. He recently won the Vuelta a Burgos, demonstrating that he’s in good stead.

Oscar Onley leads Netcompany Ineos

Oscar Onley is finally making his Grand Tour debut for Netcompany Ineos. The Scotsman was forced to miss the Tour having crashed hard at the Tour Auvergne – Rhône-Alpes. He raced to a brilliant fourth place overall in France back in 2025 and returns to the Vuelta for the first time since his DNF in 2023. This season has been difficult as aside from his Tour Auvergne – Rhône-Alpes withdrawal, he also abandoned Paris-Nice and the Tour de Romandie. Onley did win a stage and finish second overall in his last race of the Vuelta a Burgos though, just five seconds in arrears of Gall.

Josh Tarling will also be present and I’m keeping him in my thoughts for the entirety of this race. His brother Finlay Tarling died at the Volta a Portugal just last week after a non-race car got onto the course.

Lidl-Trek balancing Skjelmose and Pedersen (again)

It was a combination that worked pretty well at the Tour. Mattias Skjelmose, thought to be below new signings Juan Ayuso and Derek Gee-West in the GC hierarchy, proved himself in France by finishing sixth overall as teammate Mads Pedersen won a stage and the points classification.

The dynamic duo returns in Spain. Skjelmose is again their man for GC as Lidl-Trek insist Pedersen is ‘not specifically’ chasing green, but rather stages. Yeah, sounds like by doing the first he’ll just ride his way into the classification lead anyway.

Will Enric Mas be ol’ reliable once more?

Enric Mas comes alive on home roads in Spain. A DNF at the Tour? Doesn’t matter. He’ll end the year with a second place at the Vuelta. A terrible Giro that resulted in 32nd place in 2026? Oh lord he’s coming. Mas has amassed four podium finishes at the race and once again will be leading the team. Notably, Nairo Quintana will not be here despite his intentions of ending the career at a race he previously won in 2016.

Their teammate Cian Uijtdebroeks arrives off the back of a disappointing Tour. The Belgian suffered from illness and withdrew early on. Could the pair cook something up at the Vuelta? Genuinely, something? Anything?

A different approach for Visma-Lease a Bike

Once upon a time, Visma-Lease a Bike locked out the Vuelta podium. Sepp Kuss won his first Grand Tour in 2023, Vingegaard finished second 17sec down and Roglič completed the podium 1min 08sec behind. That won’t happen this year. Hell, there’s not much of any GC charge.

Instead the team is lead by Wout van Aert, Matthew Brennan and Kuss, the latter being the biggest hope for a solid GC placing despite racing his third Grand Tour of the year. Van Aert will look for the hilly terrain as Brennan can impress on the flatter days – particularly with only Jordi Meeus of Red Bull-Bora-Hansgrohe the purest sprinter in this edition.

Kuss was used in support of Jonas Vingegaard at both the Giro and the Tour. Once Vingegaard abandoned the latter, he could be seen going on the offensive in the final two mountain stages, fourth and third respectively on Alpe d’Huez. He last won a stage at the Vuelta in 2023 on his way to winning red. Expect to see him out front again.

The last dance

A quartet of riders will be racing in their final Vuelta before retirement at the end of the season. Pello Bilbao (Bahrain Victorious), Magnus Cort (Uno-X Mobility), Steven Kruijswijk (Visma-lease a Bike) and Jesús Herrada (Burgos Burpellet BH) will all be competing in their last Grand Tour, and it’s likely that they’ll all try to win a stage to go out with a bang.
